To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pesticide contamination of surfaces of spray equipment used in ground and aerial applications is highly variable, with the highest values observed for the hand regions.
the pesticide residue on spray equipment surfaces is a potential exposure route of operator/pilot.

(1) pesticide residues on the surface of spray equipment used in ground and aerial applications were detected by the wipe method, (2) the wipe results were higher for aerial applications than for ground applications, (3) the wipe results varied with the type of spray nozzle used in ground applications, and (4) the wipe results did not differ significantly with different types of nozzles used in aerial applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
determining how much of the operator/pilot exposure is due to contact with contaminated surfaces and how much of the exposure is directly due to the spray application process.
the determination of the extent of surface contamination of pesticide sprayers, and the estimation of potential dermal exposure to pesticide residues.

the following questions: What is the magnitude of surface contamination on the spray equipment? Is there a relationship between surface contamination and the application method? What is the relationship between the surface contamination and the work practices? What is the potential for dermal exposure of operators/pilots to the pesticides due to hand contact?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pesticide residue found on the spray equipment is not a significant contributor to operator or pilot exposure.

pesticide residue on spray equipment can contribute to the operator/pilot dermal dose, and the magnitude of that contribution will vary with the type of equipment, the work practice, and the pesticide.
pesticide residue transfer from spray equipment to hands and skin of operators or pilots is a significant factor in the determination of dermal exposure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amount of pesticide deposited on surfaces of spray equipment depends on the application method, type of spray equipment, and pesticide formulation.
the surface contamination on spray equipment was found to be a significant contributor to the total exposure of operator/pilots.
, in most cases, the contamination of the spray equipment was low and did not pose a high risk of exposure for operator/pilot.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for a better understanding of the potential exposure of operators/pilots due to the transfer of pesticide from contaminated surfaces of the spray equipment.
the surface contamination of pesticide spray equipment is a significant source of operator/pilot exposure.
the contamination levels on the spray equipment surfaces are very low, but the potential exposure of the operator due to the extended time of contact may be significant.
